title: Should I Close a Credit Card With an Annual Fee or Downgrade?
meta_description: Should I close a credit card with an annual fee or downgrade? Compare credit score impact, points and fees, plus a checklist and call script.
quick_answer: If the annual fee no longer pays for itself, downgrading is usually the lower-impact choice. A product change to a no-fee card from the same issuer typically keeps the account open, preserving its age and credit limit. Closing removes that limit, which can raise your utilization and may forfeit points. Ask about retention offers first. Closing makes most sense when no downgrade exists and other cards keep utilization low.
key_takeaways: A downgrade (product change) usually keeps the account's open date and credit limit. Closing removes that limit immediately.
Before you call, work out your utilization with and without the card. How much closing matters depends on your other limits and balances.
Ask about retention offers before you request a downgrade. They aren't guaranteed, but asking costs nothing.
Sort out your points first. Closing can forfeit issuer rewards, and a downgrade can remove options such as transfers to travel partners.
Don't say “close my account” until you're sure, and get any change confirmed in writing, because issuer rules vary.
who_this_is_for: This guide is for anyone with a rewards or travel credit card whose annual fee is coming due or has just posted, and who is deciding whether to keep paying, downgrade to a no-fee card or close the account.
intro: When a card's annual fee lands on your statement, you have three options: keep paying, downgrade to a no-fee card from the same issuer, or close the account. The choice affects more than the fee. It can change your credit utilization, the age of your credit history and whether you keep the points you've earned. This guide gives the direct answer first. Then it walks through a worked utilization example, a four-question checklist, a word-for-word call script and the pitfalls that catch people out. It explains how things generally work in the US credit system. It isn't personal financial advice, and every issuer sets its own policies, so confirm the details for your own account before you act.

steps.name: Find your fee date and refund window
steps.text: Check your latest statement or the issuer's app for the date the annual fee posts. It's usually around your account anniversary. Then check your cardholder agreement or the issuer's FAQ for a fee refund window, because some issuers refund the fee if you close or downgrade soon after it posts. Set a calendar reminder so you don't miss the window.

steps.name: Add up the benefits you actually used
steps.text: List the statement credits, rewards, insurance and perks you really used in the last 12 months. Give each one a realistic value, meaning what you would have paid out of pocket, not the figure in the card's marketing. Compare the total with the fee.

steps.name: Run your utilization numbers
steps.text: Add up the limits on all your open cards and your typical statement balances. Divide balances by limits twice: once with this card and once without it. Note whether this is your oldest account and whether you plan to apply for a loan soon.

steps.name: Protect your points
steps.text: Write down your points balance and take a screenshot. Find out whether the points would be kept, moved or forfeited if you downgrade or close. If they could be lost or lose value, redeem or transfer them first.

steps.name: Pick a downgrade target
steps.text: Look through the issuer's current no-annual-fee cards and choose one you'd actually use, ideally one whose rewards fit alongside your other cards. Co-branded airline and hotel cards may have limited downgrade options, or none.

steps.name: Ask about retention offers first
steps.text: Contact the issuer by phone, secure message or chat. Ask whether any retention offers are available on your account. Before you accept one, get the exact terms, including any spending requirement and when the offer posts.

steps.name: Request the product change
steps.text: If no offer makes the fee worth paying, ask to switch to the no-fee card you picked. Before you agree, confirm that your credit limit and open date carry over. Also ask whether your card number or APR changes, whether there's a hard inquiry, what happens to your points and any promotional balance, and whether the fee will be refunded.

steps.name: Get confirmation and follow up
steps.text: Ask for written confirmation and note the date and any reference number. Check your next statement and your credit report. If the card number changed, update autopay, subscriptions and digital wallets. Put a small recurring charge on the new card so it stays active.

sections.heading: Should I close a credit card with an annual fee or downgrade?
paragraphs: If the annual fee no longer pays for itself, downgrading is usually the lower-impact option, because the account typically stays open with its history and credit limit intact. Closing tends to make more sense when no downgrade exists or the card is causing real problems.

The formal name for a downgrade is a product change. Instead of applying for a new card, you ask the issuer to convert your existing account into another card from its lineup, usually a no-annual-fee version. Because it's the same account, the open date, payment history and credit limit usually carry over, and most issuers don't treat it as a new application. Some issuers give you a new card number and others keep the old one.

Closing works differently. The account shuts, its limit stops counting toward your available credit, and any perks or unredeemed rewards tied to the card can disappear. The account's history doesn't vanish the day you close it, but you lose the ongoing benefit of an open, well-managed credit line.

How much this matters depends on the rest of your credit file. If you have several other cards with generous limits and you pay in full, closing one card may make little visible difference. Closing tends to matter more if the card is your oldest, one of only two cards, or a large share of your total credit limit.
bullets: Keep and pay: this makes sense only if the benefits you actually use, plus any retention offer, are worth more than the fee.
Downgrade: the fee goes away and the premium perks end, but the account usually stays open with its age and limit.
Close: the fee and the credit line both go, you may lose points, and your utilization can rise depending on your other cards.

sections.heading: How closing a card affects utilization and credit history: a worked example
paragraphs: Closing a credit card usually raises your credit utilization ratio, because your balances stay the same while your total available credit shrinks.

Credit utilization is your total card balances divided by your total card limits. Widely used scoring models treat it as an important factor, and lower utilization generally signals lower risk. It's usually based on the balances your issuers report, often your statement balance. That means it can look high even if you pay in full every month.

Here's an example with made-up numbers. You have two cards. Card A has an annual fee and a $6,000 limit. Card B has no fee and a $4,000 limit. Your statement balances add up to $2,000 against $10,000 in total limits, so your utilization is 20%.

If you close Card A, you still owe $2,000, but your total limit drops to $4,000, so utilization jumps to 50%. If you downgrade Card A instead and it keeps its $6,000 limit, utilization stays at 20%. You spent the same amount, but the ratio is very different.

Now change one detail. Suppose Card B is one of several other cards with $44,000 in combined limits. Closing Card A would then move your utilization from 4% ($2,000 of $50,000) to about 4.5% ($2,000 of $44,000). That small change is why the answer depends on your other cards and balances.

Credit history changes more slowly. In the US, the credit bureaus generally say a closed account in good standing can stay on your report for up to 10 years. While it's there, it usually still counts toward the age of your accounts. Once it drops off, your average account age can fall, which shows most if it was your oldest card. A downgrade avoids this because the account never closes.

Scoring models differ, and credit reporting works differently outside the US, so treat this as an explanation of the usual mechanics, not a prediction of your score. If you're planning to apply for a mortgage, car loan or other major credit in the next few months, it's generally sensible to put off changes that could raise your utilization until afterwards.
bullets: Add up the credit limits on all your open cards.
Add up your typical monthly statement balances.
Divide balances by limits twice: once with the card you're thinking of closing and once without it.
Check whether this card is your oldest account.
Note any major credit application you plan to make in the next few months.

sections.heading: Decision checklist: four questions to answer before you call
paragraphs: Most annual-fee decisions come down to four questions: Do the benefits you use cover the fee? Is a retention offer available? Is there a no-fee card to downgrade to? What happens to your points?

1. Do the benefits you use cover the fee? Count only the value you really got in the last 12 months: statement credits you used, rewards you redeemed, and insurance or lounge access you relied on. Leave out credits you'd have to go out of your way to use. For rewards, count only the extra you earned compared with what a no-fee card would have earned on the same spending, valued at what you actually redeem points for.

Here's a hypothetical example. A card has a $250 annual fee. You used a $100 travel credit on a trip you'd have taken anyway. You earned about $90 more in rewards than a no-fee card would have. You used a lounge once, which you value at $20. That's roughly $210 of real value against a $250 fee, so the card falls short unless a retention offer makes up the difference.

2. Is a retention offer available? Issuers sometimes offer statement credits, bonus points or a spending bonus to keep you as a customer. These offers aren't guaranteed and depend on the issuer, your account and the timing, but asking costs nothing. Judge any offer the same way: are the offer and the benefits you'll really use worth more than the fee?

3. Is there a no-fee card to downgrade to? Check the issuer's current no-annual-fee cards, ideally in the same card family. Co-branded airline and hotel cards sometimes have limited options, or none. Some issuers restrict product changes by card network or by how long the account has been open. A product change usually doesn't come with a welcome bonus.

4. What happens to your points? Ask whether your points stay with the account, move to the new card's rewards program or are forfeited if you close. Also ask whether a downgrade would remove any redemption options, such as transfers to travel partners.

Retention offer: the amount, any spending requirement, the deadline and when it posts
Downgrade target: the card's name, plus confirmation that your limit and open date carry over
Points: your current balance and whether the points are kept, moved or lost
The fee refund window, if the fee has already posted

sections.heading: What happens to your points, perks and balance
paragraphs: Rewards, perks and any balance you carry are the easiest things to get wrong, so sort them out before you change or close the account.

If you close a card, points in the issuer's own rewards program are often forfeited unless you redeem them or move them to another eligible card first. Miles or points earned on a co-branded card usually sit in your airline or hotel loyalty account rather than with the card, so they often survive a closure. Confirm this with both the issuer and the loyalty program.

If you downgrade, your points usually carry over, but what you can do with them may change. Some rewards programs keep transfers to travel partners or higher redemption values for their premium cards, so a downgrade can quietly lower what your points are worth. If that applies to you, consider redeeming or transferring them first.

The premium card's perks end when the card changes. Depending on the card, you could lose travel insurance, purchase and rental car coverage, lounge access, free checked bags, elite status and recurring statement credits. If you booked an upcoming trip with the card, ask whether its travel coverage still applies after the change.

A balance doesn't disappear when you close or downgrade. Ask whether your interest rate (APR) changes with the new card and whether any promotional balance transfer rate carries over. If you're paying interest, paying down the balance generally does more for your utilization, and your budget, than any card change.

Pay attention to timing. Some issuers refund the annual fee if you close or downgrade within a set period after it posts, and others don't. Some may reduce the refund or take back the value of credits you used that card year. If you opened the card recently, check whether its terms let the issuer take back a welcome bonus when an account is closed or changed soon after opening.
bullets: Take a screenshot of your current points balance.
Redeem or transfer any points that won't survive the change.
List the perks you rely on and line up replacements.
Update autopay, subscriptions and digital wallets if your card number changes.
Tell any authorized users, because their cards are affected too.

sections.heading: Call script: how to ask about retention offers and a downgrade
paragraphs: A sensible order is to ask about retention offers first and a product change second, so you hear every option before you commit to anything.

Call the number on the back of your card, or use the issuer's secure messaging or chat. Some issuers also let you request a product change online. Before you start, have your points balance, your fee date and the name of the no-fee card you want ready. Be polite and honest. You don't need to threaten to cancel.
bullets: Opening: “Hi, my annual fee [is coming up / posted on DATE], and I'm reviewing whether this card still makes sense for me. Are there any retention offers available on my account?”
If there's an offer: “What exactly is the offer, is there a spending requirement, and when would it post?”
If there's no offer: “Understood. Which no-annual-fee cards can I product change to?”
Confirm the details: “Will I keep the same open date and credit limit? Will my card number or APR change? Is there a hard credit inquiry?”
Points and fee: “What happens to my points if I downgrade, and what would happen if I closed the account? Would the annual fee be refunded in either case?”
Commit: “Please go ahead with the product change to [card name], and send me written confirmation.”
Before you hang up, note the date, the representative's name and any reference number.

sections.heading: When closing the card is the better choice
paragraphs: Closing tends to make sense when there's no reasonable downgrade option and the card isn't doing much for your credit profile, or when keeping it open causes real problems.

Typical cases look like this: the card has no no-fee version, your other cards keep utilization low without it, and it isn't your oldest account. Closing can also be reasonable if an open credit line makes overspending harder to resist, or if you simply want fewer accounts to watch for fraud.

Before you close, ask whether the issuer will move part of this card's credit limit to another card you hold with them. Some issuers allow this, which can soften the effect on your utilization. Ask whether moving the limit involves a credit check.

Closing a card to make room for a different one is a separate decision. A new application usually means a hard inquiry and a lower average account age, and approval and welcome bonus eligibility depend on each issuer's rules.

If you do close, do it carefully. Pay off the remaining balance or have a plan for it, use or move your points, move any recurring charges to another card and ask for written confirmation. A month or two later, check your credit report to make sure the account shows as closed at your request.

Be careful with the words “close my account” on the phone. A representative may close the account on the spot, and reopening it isn't guaranteed. If you're undecided, “Thanks, I'll think about it” is a perfectly good way to end the call.

Downgrades carry a quieter risk. If you never use the no-fee card, the issuer may eventually close it for inactivity, which affects your utilization in the same way. A common way to keep it active is to put one small recurring charge on it and pay it with autopay.
bullets: The card has no no-fee version in its family.
Your other cards keep your utilization low without this card's limit.
It isn't your oldest account.
You aren't planning a major loan application in the next few months.
Having the credit line open makes overspending or debt more likely.

sections.heading: Issuer policies vary: what to confirm before you decide
paragraphs: Every issuer sets its own rules for product changes, retention offers, fee refunds and points, and those rules change over time. Confirm the details for your own account instead of relying on general guidance, including this article.
Start with your cardholder agreement and the issuer's website, then use the call to fill in the gaps. Get anything important in writing, such as a secure message or a confirmation email.

Credit reporting also varies by country. The explanations here reflect typical US practice. If you live elsewhere, check guidance from your local credit reference agencies or financial regulator. If the decision is tied to a mortgage, paying off debt or your wider financial plans, a licensed adviser or a reputable non-profit credit counselor can review your full situation.

faq.question: Does downgrading a credit card hurt your credit score?
faq.answer: A downgrade usually has little effect on your credit, because the account stays open with the same open date and, usually, the same credit limit. Most issuers don't treat a product change as a new application, so there's typically no hard inquiry. Policies vary, so confirm the limit and inquiry details with your issuer before you agree to the change.

faq.question: Will I lose my points if I downgrade my credit card?
faq.answer: Usually not. Points often carry over, but you may lose redemption options such as transfers to travel partners, which can lower what your points are worth. Ask your issuer exactly what changes, and if you're unsure, redeem or transfer your points before the downgrade.

faq.question: Can I get my annual fee refunded if I close or downgrade my card?
faq.answer: Some issuers refund the annual fee if you close or downgrade within a set period after it posts, and others don't. Some may also reduce the refund or take back the value of credits you used. Check your cardholder agreement or ask when you call.

faq.question: How long does a closed credit card stay on my credit report?
faq.answer: In the US, the credit bureaus generally say a closed account in good standing can stay on your report for up to 10 years. Negative items such as late payments generally stay for about seven years. Reporting rules are different in other countries, so check with your local credit reference agencies.

faq.question: Is it better to close a credit card or keep it open with no balance?
faq.answer: If the card has no fee, keeping it open and using it now and then usually helps your utilization and credit age. If the card has a fee, a downgrade often keeps those benefits without the cost. Closing can still be reasonable if there's no downgrade option or if having the card open makes overspending more likely.

faq.question: Can I upgrade back to the premium card later?
faq.answer: Some issuers allow a product change back to a premium card, but it isn't guaranteed and depends on their rules at the time. An upgrade usually doesn't come with a welcome bonus. If this matters to you, ask your issuer before you downgrade.

conclusion: When an annual fee no longer pays for itself, start by asking your issuer about retention offers. If none is worth taking, a product change to a no-fee card from the same issuer usually ends the fee and keeps the account's age and credit limit. Closing tends to make sense only after you've worked out your utilization, sorted out your points and confirmed there's no sensible downgrade option. Issuer policies and credit rules vary, so check the details for your own account. For decisions tied to a major loan or your wider financial plans, talk to a licensed adviser or a reputable non-profit credit counselor.
